raw_case_text:
A 93-year-old Caucasian woman was referred to the Internal Medicine Consultation due to cervical adenopathies with 3 months duration. With respect to past medical history, 4 years earlier she had been diagnosed with cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face and submitted to surgical excision. The patient denied having fever, asthenia, fatigue, weight loss or night sweats; furthermore, there were no respiratory symptoms. She denied having a previous history of tuberculosis (TB) and recent contact with people with known or suspected TB. There was no epidemiological context or contact with animals. On physical examination, an enlarged, mobile and painful right cervical lymph node was evident; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.
Cervico-thoraco-abdominal-pelvic computed tomography (CT) showed a right cervical mass (Fig. 1) with multiple adenopathies and some fibrotic lesions in the upper right lobe; there were no other adenopathies nor evidence of neoplastic disease. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of the cervical node was performed and yielded a noncaseous granulomatous process. There was no evidence of Reed-Sternberg cells or neoplastic cells; Ziehl-Neelsen staining was negative, as well as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assessment for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MT) and culture. The patient was kept under close surveillance. In the meantime, an IgG lambda monoclonal gammopathy was diagnosed; renal function and calcium metabolism were normal, there was no anaemia or elevated urinary free light chains and beta-2 microglobulin was normal. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping demonstrated a polyclonal B cell population. In addition, serology tests for syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus were negative, and QuantiFERON testing was positive. Two months later, the adenopathies had grown and there was cutaneous fistulization with suppurative lymphadenitis (Figs. 2A and 2B).
Microbiologic examination of a suppuration swab was positive for Staphylococcus aureus and the patient was treated with cefuroxime, displaying only slight improvement. An excisional biopsy was programmed and histological examination revealed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration.
PCR assessment of the samples was negative for MT, Nocardia, Mycobacterium avium complex, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum and Leishmania infantum. Considering the presence of persistent cervical lymphadenopathy with caseous granulomas, a positive QuantiFERON test, and the exclusion of other potential causes, the hypothesis of cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis was strongly suspected, even without a positive PCR test for MT. The patient started presumptive treatment with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Afterwards, diagnostic confirmation was obtained by isolation of MT in one of the lymph node cultures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing did not demonstrate resistances. The patient presented a favourable clinical outcome with gradual reduction in the size of the adenopathies and there were no side effects attributable to the antituberculous drugs.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 93-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 3-month history of painful right cervical lymphadenopathy that subsequently progressed to cutaneous fistulization and suppuration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred to internal medicine for a 3-month history of right cervical adenopathy without constitutional or respiratory symptoms. Over the ensuing 2 months of surveillance, the cervical nodes enlarged and fistulized to the skin with purulent drainage (growing secondary Staphylococcus aureus with minimal response to cefuroxime).
subjective.past_medical_history: Cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face surgically excised 4 years earlier; newly identified incidental IgG lambda monoclonal gammopathy; no prior tuberculosis history, TB contacts, or animal exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right neck pain and subsequent purulent drainage; negative for fever, asthenia, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, or respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Enlarged, mobile, tender right cervical lymphadenopathy that progressed 2 months later to cutaneous fistulization and suppurative lymphadenitis; remainder of physical exam was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed an IgG lambda monoclonal gammopathy with polyclonal B cells on peripheral immunophenotyping, normal hemoglobin, renal function, calcium, urinary free light chains, and beta-2 microglobulin, negative serologies for HIV, HBV, HCV, and syphilis, and a positive QuantiFERON-TB test; swab of the fistula drainage grew Staphylococcus aureus.
objective.advanced_workup: Cervico-thoraco-abdominopelvic CT showed a right cervical nodal mass, multiple cervical adenopathies, and right upper lobe pulmonary fibrotic lesions without malignancy. Initial cervical lymph node FNA showed non-caseating granulomas (negative Ziehl-Neelsen stain, MTB PCR, and culture); subsequent excisional lymph node biopsy revealed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration, negative PCR for Leishmania infantum, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, MAC, Nocardia, Toxoplasma, Aspergillus, Bartonella, and Treponema pallidum, and a positive lymph node culture isolating pan-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, and infectious lymphadenitis due to Leishmania infantum, Nocardia, MAC, Bartonella, or fungi were excluded; caseating granulomas on excisional biopsy, positive QuantiFERON-TB, and isolation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in lymph node culture confirmed cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis (scrofula). Standard four-drug antitubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) produced steady regression of the cervical lymphadenopathy without adverse drug events.
